cards.note:
Albanian belongs to its own branch of the Indo-European languages, and is thus not closely related to any other European language. The use of letter Ë ë is a distinct feature for Albanian. Sometimes, you'll find the letter Ç ç too.

The Albanian word for street is rruga.

NOTE: Albanian is also the majority language in Kosovo, and recognized as a minority language in North Macedonia and Montenegro.

Catalan is a Romance language closely related to Spanish and French. It is the main language in Andorra, but spoken in bordering regions of both Spain and France, most notably Catalonia in Spain.

If you are unfamiliar with Romance languages, it can be hard to distinguish between Catalan and Spanish. If you see i instead of y (“and” in English), it is Catalan. In addition, more Catalan words end with consonants.

The Catalan word for street is carrer.

German is a Germanic language related to Dutch, and the official language of Austria. The German language uses the special letters Ä, Ö, Ü and ẞ.

The German word for street is Straße.

The German word for road is Weg (same as Dutch).

NOTE: Alongside Austria, German is the majority language in Germany, Switzerland and Liechtenstein, and has regional majority in eastern Belgium and the Italian province of South Tyrol.
Brussels is the capital city of Belgium and officially bilingual in French and Dutch (Flemish). Brussels street signs include both the French rue and Dutch straat.

Dutch, often referred to as Flemish within Belgium, is a Germanic language. In Belgium, Dutch is spoken in the northern Flanders region, and alongside French in the capital city of Brussels.

Dutch features a lot of double vowels. Typical letter clusters are ij, ieuw and oe. “IJ“ written as one capitalised letter is also unique to the language.

The Dutch name for street is straat.

NOTE: Dutch is the main language of the Netherlands.

French is a Romance language closely related to languages like Catalan, Spanish and Italian. In Belgium, French is spoken in the southern Wallonia region, and alongside Dutch in the capital city of Brussels.

The French word for street is rue.

French uses these diacritics and special letters:

  • Accent aigu: é
  • Accent grave: à, è, ù
  • Accent circonflexe: â, ê, î, ô, û
  • Trema: ë, ï, ü, ÿ
  • Ligature: œ
  • Cédille: ç with a small hook

In addition, the -ux suffix is only found in French.

NOTE: French is also widely spoken in France, Luxembourg, Switzerland and Monaco.

There are three versions of the Serbo-Croatian language recognized in Bosnia and Herzegovina: Bosnian, Serbian and Croatian. Speakers consider them separate languages though, and base the split on the ethnicity of the user: Bosniak, Serb or Croat. Serbian (and Bosnian technically) use either Latin or Cyrillic, while Croatian always uses the Latin script. In practice, it is only in Serbian-majority regions (mostly in Republika Srpska) where you will find Cyrillic.

NOTE: Serbian is also commonly written with Latin script, and thus might be indistinguishable from Bosnian/Croatian.

ALSO NOTE: Official road signs may use both scripts nation-wide.

The Serbo-Croatian word for street is ulica (like most Slavic languages).

There are three versions of the Serbo-Croatian language recognized in Bosnia and Herzegovina: Bosnian, Serbian and Croatian. Speakers consider them separate languages though, and base the split on the ethnicity of the user: Bosniak, Serb or Croat. Serbian (and Bosnian technically) use either Latin or Cyrillic, while Croatian always uses the Latin script. In practice, it is only in Serbian-majority regions (mostly in Republika Srpska) where you will find Cyrillic.

NOTE: Serbian is also commonly written with Latin script, and thus might be indistinguishable from Bosnian/Croatian.

ALSO NOTE: Official road signs may use both scripts nation-wide.

The Serbo-Croatian word for street is улица/ulica (like most Slavic languages).

Bulgarian is a South Slavic language, closely related to Macedonian. Bulgarian mainly uses the Cyrillic alphabet, but many signs are written in both Cyrillic and Latin scripts. The letter Ъ is only found in Bulgarian and Russian, although it is fairly uncommon in Russian, and is thus a good way to identify Bulgarian.

The Bulgarian word for street is улица (ulitsa), sometimes abbreviated ул. (ul.). This is the same as most Slavic languages (Russian, Serbian...).

Croatian is the version of Serbo-Croatian official in Croatia. It is always written in the Latin script, unlike Bosnian, Montenegrin and, especially, Serbian which may use Cyrillic. Serbo-Croatian is also related to Slovene spoken in Slovenia, and may look very similar. Slovene and Serbo-Croatian both use the special characters Č, Š and Ž, but only Serbo-Croatian uses Ć and Đ aswell.

The Croatian word for street is ulica (like most Slavic languages).

Slovene and Serbo-Croatian written in Latin (South Slavic) may look similar to Czech and Slovak (West Slavic). One of the best ways to know it is a South Slavic language is to look for extensive use of letter combinations including the letter j, such as lj or nj. The Slovenian Capital of Ljubljana is a great example.

Cyprus (the Republic of Cyprus) mainly uses the Greek language. Greek has a unique alphabet not used in any other language. It shares similarities with both the Latin and Cyrillic alphabets, however the lower case letters generally have softer shapes than the Cyrillic letters. English is also common to find on the island, due to Cyprus' history as a British Colony. The UK still holds on to the Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia, which also have a bit of official coverage.

NOTE: To distinguish Cyprus from Greece, remember that Cyprus drives on the left.

Czech is a West Slavic language, mutually intelligible with Slovak. Czech and Slovak both use the special letters Č, Ď, Ň, Š, Ť, Á, É, Í, Ó, Ú and Ý. However, they both have some distinct letters that can be used to tell them apart:

  • Czech: Ř, Ě and Ů;
  • Slovak: Ľ, Ô, Ä, Ŕ and Ĺ.

The Czech word for street is ulice, unlike ulica used in Slovak (and most other Slavic langauges). Most street signs in Czechia don't include any word meaning street, however. What you can learn instead is that if you see ulica, it will never be Czechia.

NOTE: Acute accents on vowels (Á, É, Í, Ó, Ú and Ý) are not found in South Slavic languages (Slovene, Serbo-Croatian).

Danish is a North Germanic language, closely related to Norwegian and Swedish. The Danish alphabet contains the special letters Æ, Ø, and Å.

NOTE:

  • Norwegian also uses Æ, Ø, and Å.
  • Faroese uses Æ and Ø but not Å.
  • Icelandic only uses Æ.
  • Swedish only uses Å. In addition, Swedish uses Ä and Ö, which are not found in Danish.

The Danish word for road is vej. This is unlike Swedish which uses väg or vägen and Norwegian which uses vei/veien or veg/vegen (depending on spelling).

The Danish word for street is gade. This is unlike Swedish which uses gata or gatan and Norwegian which uses gate, gata or rarely gaten.

Estonian is a Finnic language closely related to Finnish. It is not related to Latvian or Lithuanian. Within the Baltic languages, the following letters are unique to Estonian:

  • Vowels with umlauts (two dots): Ä, Ö, and Ü. Ä and Ö also exist in Finnish, but not Ü.
  • Õ with a tilde. This letter is one of the best ways to identify Estonian. Portuguese also uses it however, but mixing up Estonian and Portuguese is hard because they are otherwise very different.

The Estonian word for street is tänav, very commonly abbreviated as tn.

The Estonian word for road is tee. This is unlike Finnish which uses tie.

Faroese is a North Germanic Language most closely related to Icelandic. It uses the special letters Á, Ð, Í, Ó, Ú, Ý, Æ and Ø. It differs from Icelandic by using the letter Ø, while Icelandic uses É and Þ.

Finnish is a Finnic language closely related to Estonian. It is completely unrelated to all other major Nordic languages. The Finnish alphabet includes the letters Ä and Ö. While these are also used in Swedish, Finnish can be told apart from it by the many long words and especially the double vowels, which are rare in Swedish.

Estonian, to which Finnish is closely related, uses the letters Õ and Ü plus the same Ä and Ö as in Finnish.

The Finnish word for road is tie. This is unlike Estonian which uses tee instead.

The Finnish word for street is katu.

In some coastal areas of southern and western Finland, you will find bilingual signs in Finnish and Swedish. Street signs in these regions typically include both -tie and -vägen (meaning road) or both -katu and -gatan (meaning street).

NOTE: Swedish is also spoken monolingually on the Åland Islands (and in Sweden, of course).

French is a Romance language closely related to languages like Catalan, Spanish and Italian.

The French word for street is rue.

French uses these diacritics and special letters:

  • Accent aigu: é
  • Accent grave: à, è, ù
  • Accent circonflexe: â, ê, î, ô, û
  • Trema: ë, ï, ü, ÿ
  • Ligature: œ
  • Cédille: ç with a small hook

In addition, the -ux suffix is only found in French.

NOTE: French is also widely spoken in Belgium, Luxembourg, Switzerland and Monaco.

Georgian is a Kartvelian language and the official language of Georgia. The Georgian script is overall quite swirly and unique, not resembling any other European language. On directional signs, Latin script is very commonly used alongside Georgian.

NOTE: It is possible to confuse Georgian and other swirly scripts found in Asia. Georgia should however look fairly different from these countries (like India, for example). As a former member of the Soviet Union, Georgia still has visible similarities with Russia when it comes to infrastructure and more.

German is a Germanic language related to Dutch. The German language uses the special letters Ä, Ö, Ü and ß.

The German word for street is Straße.

The German word for road is Weg (same as Dutch).

Alongside Germany, German is the majority language in Austria, Switzerland and Liechtenstein, and has regional majority in eastern Belgium and the Italian province of South Tyrol.

The Greek language features a unique alphabet not used in any other language. It shares similarities with both the Latin and Cyrillic alphabets, however the lower case letters generally have softer shapes than the Cyrillic letters.

NOTE: Cyprus also uses the Greek alphabet, but drives on the left.

Hungarian is a Ugric language that is unrelated to all its surrounding languages. It has a unique look, with a large number of acute accents (Á, É, Í, Ó, Ú), umlauts (Ö, Ü), and long words. The letters Ő and Ű, with double acute accents, are unique to the language.

The Hungarian name for street is utca. The word út is also used for bigger roads. No other language shares this name.

NOTE: Hungarian is widely spoken is parts of neighboring countries, notably Romania and Slovakia.

Icelandic is a North Germanic language, most closely related to Faroese. Icelandic uses vowels with acute accents (Á, É, Í, Ó, Ú, Ý), and the special letters Þ, Ð (lowercase: ð), Æ and Ö. Faroese does not use Þ, É or Ö, but uses Ø instead.

Irish is a Celtic language native to the island of Ireland and co-official with English in the Republic of Ireland. Irish signage is often bilingual, with English in a regular font, and Irish in italics. Place names, regular words and phrases are all translated. Irish language is somewhat less common on non-official signage.

Italian is a Romance language and the most spoken language in Italy. Italian does not use any real special letters, only accents on top of vowels: (À, È, É, Ì, Ò, Ó and Ù).

The Italian word for street is via.

Italian is perhaps most often confused with Spanish. Some characteristics of Italian that can help with this distinction are:

  • Extensive use of double consonants
  • Extensive use of the letter i
  • Almost all words ending in a vowel

Take the text in the picture below as an example. In Italian, this text has 5 uses of double vowels, 28 uses of the letter i and 29 words ending in a vowel. The same numbers for the Spanish version are 0, 6 and 6 respectively.

Kosovo has two official languages: Albanian and Serbian. About 90% of the population identify as Albanian and the Albanian language is by far the most common in Kosovo. In Serb-majority regions, mostly the northern part of Kosovo, you will find Serbian instead.

Street signs in Kosovo generally say RR./UL., including the Albanian rruga and the Serbian ulica.

Albanian belongs to its own branch of the Indo-European languages, and is thus not closely related to any other European language. The use of letter Ë ë is a distinct feature for Albanian. Sometimes, you'll find the letter Ç ç too.

Latvian is a Baltic language closely related to Lithuanian. Within the Baltic languages, the following letters are unique to Latvian:

  • Vowels with a macron (horizontal stripe): Ā Ē Ī (both Latvian and Lithuanain use Ū however).
  • Consonants with a small hook: Ģ Ķ Ļ Ņ (Lithuanian has similar hooks connected to the bottom of vowels).

The Latvian word for street is iela. This word is unique to Latvian.

NOTE: Estonian is not a part of the Baltic language family (despite the name), but rather a Finnic language related to Finnish.

Lithuanian is a Baltic language closely related to Latvian. Within the Baltic languages, the following letters are unique to Lithuanian:

  • Vowels with small hooks: Ą Ę Į Ų (Latvian uses similar hooks under some consonants).
  • Ė with a single dot.
  • Y (also in Estonian, but only in loan words).

The Lithuanian word for street is gatve, often abbreviated as g. on signs.

Lithuanian place names often end in -ai.

NOTE: Estonian is not a part of the Baltic language family (despite the name), but rather a Finnic language related to Finnish.

cards.a: Luxembourg  - Luxembourgish (+presence of French and German)
cards.note:
Luxembourg is a country with an interesting mix of languages. The national language is Luxembourgish, a Germanic language closely related to German. Like German, it uses umlauts (dots over vowels). In addition, it uses a fair amount of double vowels, and sometimes an é with an accent.

French and German are also used as administrative languages in Luxembourg alongside Luxembourgish. French is the language mostly used for public communication. Road signs and advertisements are usually in French. Presence of German on signs is less common compared to French, but certainly not non-existent.

While English is the primary language of Malta, it is also common to see the Maltese language. Maltese is a Semitic language sharing its origin with Arabic, but written with the Latin script and heavily influenced by Italian. Unique letters for Maltese include Ċ, Ġ, Ż and Ħ.

The Maltese word for street is triq, which can be seen on almost every street sign in Malta.

Montenegrin is a South Slavic language and the only version of Serbo-Croatian official in Montenegro. However, Serbian is technically the most widely spoken language in Montenegro, ahead of Montenegrin. For the purpose of this map, these two languages might aswell be the same (they are that similar). Both Montenegrin and Serbian are officially written either in Latin or Cyrillic, but Latin is by far the more common script used in Montenegro. Road signs are not required to use both scripts, only Latin. Montenegrin uses the letters Ś and Ź which can not be found in Croatian/Bosnian/Serbian.

The Serbo-Croatian word for street is ulica/улица (like most Slavic languages).

Dutch is a Germanic language related to German. Dutch features a lot of double vowels. Typical letter clusters are ij, ieuw and oe. “IJ“ written as one capitalised letter is also unique to the language.

The Dutch name for street is straat.

The Dutch name for road is weg (same as German).

NOTE: Dutch is also spoken in the northern Flanders region of Belgium.

Macedonian is a South Slavic language closely related to Bulgarian. Macedonian uses the Cyrillic script. Road signs have Latin on them too, although most other signs are fully in Cyrillic.

The letters Ѓ and Ќ are unique to Macedonian. Љ, Њ, and Џ are only used in Serbo-Croatian and Macedonian (not in Bulgarian). The same goes for the letter J (loaned from Latin), where Й is used in Bulgarian instead. Bulgarian uses the letter Ъ which is not found in Macedonian or Serbo-Croatian.

The Macedonian word for street is улица (ulitsa), like most Slavic languages.

Norwegian is a North Germanic language closely related to Danish and Swedish. The Norwegian alphabet contains these special letters: Æ, Ø, and Å.

NOTE:

  • Danish also uses Æ, Ø, and Å.
  • Swedish only uses Å. In addition, Swedish uses Ä and Ö, not found in Norwegian. Norwegian uses more E’s than Swedish, while Swedish uses more A’s. Norwegian uses kk where Swedish uses ck.
  • Faroese uses Æ and Ø but not Å.
  • Icelandic only uses Æ.

The Norwegian word for road is vei or veien (or veg/vegen, depending on spelling). This is unlike Swedish which uses väg or vägen and Danish which uses vej.

The Norwegian word for street is gate, gata or rarely gaten. In Swedish it is gatan or, sometimes, gata aswell. Danish uses gade.

Polish is a West Slavic language related to Czech and Slovak. In contrast to other Slavic languages, the Polish alphabet includes:

  • Ł with a stroke through it (unique to Polish)
  • Ą and Ę with a small hook (also found in Lithuanian)
  • Ć, Ń, Ó, Ś, Ź with an acute accent. Of these, Ń is unique to Polish. In addition, the only other language with Ś and Ź is Montenegrin.
  • Ż with a small dot (unique to Polish)

Polish is very consonant-heavy, with lots of consonant clusters. Polish does not use V. Instead, it uses W a lot, the only Slavic language to do so. Other unusually common consonants are the Z, K, and C.

The Polish word for street is ulica, abbreviated ul. (like most other Slavic languages).

Portuguese is a Romance language closely related to Spanish. Spanish and Portuguese can look very similar. Some key differences between the two:

  • Ñ is unique to Spanish.
  • Ç, Ã, Õ, Â, Ê and lh are unique to Portuguese (Ç is also present in Catalan).
  • Portuguese uses the -ao word ending, and -nh- instead of ñ.
  • Spanish uses de and del, while these are often contracted to da, do, das and dos in Portuguese.

The Portuguese word for road is Rua.

Romanian is a Romance language similar to Italian, containing the special letters: Ă, Ș and Ț.

These letters are found in Romanian aswell as some other European languages:

  • Â, used in French, Portuguese and Turkish
  • Î, used in French, Turkish and Italian

Additionally, in Turkish you can find the letter Ş, which can be confused with the Romanian Ș.

The Romanian word for street is strada, abbreviated as str. Keep in mind that the German Straße also might be abbreviated str.

Russian is an East Slavic language related to Ukrainian and Belarusian. Russian uses the Cyrillic script, and contains the special letters Ы, Э, Ё and Ъ. Ё is also used in Mongolian and Ъ is used in Bulgarian (where it's more common).

The Russian word for street is улица (ulitsa), sometimes abbreviated ул. (ul.). Most other Slavic languages also use улица/ulica. The Ukrainian word however is вулиця (vulytsya), abbreviated вул. (vul.).

The Russian word for city is город (gorod), abbreviated г. (g.). The Ukrainian word is instead місто (misto), abbreviated м. (m.).

Serbian is the version of Serbo-Croatian official in Serbia. Serbian uses both the Cyrillic and Latin script, and most official road signs use both scripts. Croatian will never use Cyrillic, while Bosnian and Montenegrin might. These letters are unique to Serbo-Croatian (Cyrillic): Ђ ђ and Ћ ћ.

These letters are found in Serbo-Croatian and Macedonian: Љ љ, Њ њ and Џ џ. The J from Latin is also used in Cyrillic in these languages (in Bulgarian or Russian, Й is used instead).

The Serbo-Croatian word for street is улица/ulica (like most Slavic languages).

Slovak is a West Slavic language mutually intelligible with Czech. Czech and Slovak both use the special letters Č, Ď, Ň, Š, Ť, Á, É, Í, Ó, Ú and Ý. However, they both have some distinct letters that can be used to tell them apart:

  • Czech: Ř, Ě and Ů;
  • Slovak: Ľ, Ô, Ä, Ŕ and Ĺ.

The Slovak word for street is ulica (like most Slavic languages). In Czech it is ulice instead, but most street signs in Czechia don't include any word meaning street. What you can learn instead is that if you see ulica, it will never be Czechia.

NOTE: Acute accents on vowels (Á, É, Í, Ó, Ú and Ý) are not found in South Slavic languages (Slovene, Serbo-Croatian).

Slovene is a South Slavic language closely related to Serbo-Croatian (Croatian, Serbian, Bosnian, Montenegrin). Slovene features the special letters Č, Š, and Ž. Croatian has these aswell, but also uses Ć and Đ which don't exist in Slovene.

The Slovene word for school is šola, while Croatian is škola. This can commonly be found painted on roads.

The Slovene word for street is ulica (like most Slavic languages).

Slovene and Serbo-Croatian written in Latin (South Slavic) may look similar to Czech and Slovak (West Slavic). One of the best ways to know it is a South Slavic language is to look for extensive use of letter combinations including the letter j, such as lj or nj. The Slovenian Capital of Ljubljana is a great example.

Basque is a language isolate spoken in adjacent parts of northern Spain and southwestern France. It has a unique look, not resembling any other language, commonly including the letters K, X and Z. In Spain, you will find a mix of Spanish and Basque signs (often bilingual) in the Basque Country and northern Navarre.

Streets in Basque-speaking areas of Spain are sometimes called kalea (in France karrika instead). However, Spanish calle is also still common.

Catalan is a Romance language closely related to Spanish and French. In Spain, it is spoken in Catalonia, the Valencian Community, and the Balearic Islands. In Catalonia and the Balearic Islands, it is (much) more common than Spanish on signage. The Valencian Community is more bilingual.

The Catalan word for street is carrer. This is unlike Spainsh where it is calle.

If you are unfamiliar with Romance languages, it can otherwise be hard to distinguish between Catalan and Spanish. If you see i instead of y (“and” in English), it is Catalan. In addition, more Catalan words end with consonants.

Spanish is a Romance language closely related to Portuguese. Spanish and Portuguese can look very similar. Some key differences between the two:

  • Ñ is unique to Spanish.
  • Ç, Ã, Õ, Â, Ê and lh are unique to Portuguese (Ç is also present in Catalan).
  • Portuguese uses the -ao word ending, and -nh- instead of ñ.
  • Spanish uses de and del, while these are often contracted to da, do, das and dos in Portuguese.

The Spanish word for street is calle.

Swedish is a North Germanic language closely related to Danish and Norwegian. The Swedish alphabet contains these special letters: Å, Ä, and Ö.

NOTE:

  • Danish and Norwegian use Å but not Ä or Ö, instead using Æ and Ø.
  • Icelandic uses Ö, but not Å or Ä
  • Norwegian uses more E’s than Swedish, while Swedish uses more A’s. Norwegian uses kk where Swedish uses ck.

You can also find Ä and Ö in Finnish, but Finnish is not a Germanic language and therefore looks quite different from Swedish.

The Swedish word for road is väg or vägen. This is unlike Norwegian which uses vei or veien (or veg/vegen, depending on spelling) and Danish which uses vej.

The Swedish word for street is gata or, more commonly, gatan. Norwegian might also use gata or gate/gaten and Danish uses gade.

Switzerland has four official languages spoken in their own regions of the country. French is the second most spoken language in Switzerland after German. It is spoken in western parts of the country. You can often use place names on the map to tell what language is spoken where.

NOTE: Some areas, mostly near language borders, are bilingual.

Switzerland has four official languages spoken in their own regions of the country. German is the most widely spoken language in Switzerland. It is (mostly) spoken in central and northern parts of the country. You can often use place names on the map to tell what language is spoken where.

NOTE: Some areas, mostly near language borders, are bilingual.

ALSO NOTE: Unlike Germany and Austria, Swiss German does not use the letter ß, replacing it by ss in words like Straße (street), becoming Strasse in Swiss German.

Switzerland has four official languages spoken in their own regions of the country. Italian is spoken in southern parts of the country, close to Italy. You can often use place names on the map to tell what language is spoken where.

NOTE: Some areas, mostly near language borders, are bilingual.

Turkish is a Turkic language related to Azerbaijani and Turkmen. The Turkish language has a fairly unique look. It uses the following special characters:

  • Ç and Ş with a cedilla (“hook” below the letter).
  • Ö and Ü with an umlaut (two dots).
  • Ğ with a breve.
  • Dotless I ı. This letter in particular is noteworthy, as it is essentially unique to Turkish. In case you are confused: this is similar to the letter i, but without a dot when written in lowercase.
  • Capital İ with a dot.

Stop signs in Türkiye say DUR instead of STOP. This is unique to Türkiye.

Another common word to see is belediyesi, meaning municipality. One of the places you will find this word is on bins, and of course this will also give you place name info.

Ukrainian is an East Slavic language related to Russian and Belarusian. Ukrainian uses the Cyrillic script. These letters are unique to Ukrainian, compared to Russian: Ґ ґ, І і, Ї ї and Є є (not to be confused with Э э in Russian and Belarusian).

The Ukrainian word for street is вулиця (vulytsya), abbreviated вул. (vul.). The Russian word is улица (ulitsa), abbreviated ул. (ul.), without a в (v) at the beginning.

The Ukrainian word for city is місто (misto), abbreviated м. (m.). It can be used both to differentiate it from Russian where the word for city is город (gorod), abbreviated г. (g.), and to quickly find the city name in addresses.

English is the main language of the United Kingdom (I bet you knew that already). Keep in mind that English is also spoken in Ireland, aswell as Malta and Gibraltar within Europe. It is not uncommon to find English in other countries aswell, where is acts as an international language.

Scottish Gaelic is a Celtic language closely related to Irish. They have a very similar look and use accent marks commonly. Common and recognizable letter clusters include bh, dh, fh, mh, ai, ea, eo, and ui.

Scottish Gaelic on road signs is found most commonly in the Scottish Highlands, and is almost always found north of Glasgow.

NOTE: Scottish Gaelic on road signs will often be in green or yellow text. This will not happen with Welsh or Irish on road signs.

Welsh is a Celtic language spoken throughout Wales. Road signs in Wales are usually bilingual English and Welsh. Towns often have Welsh names too.

Welsh uses the letters D, W, and Y much more commonly than English. The double LL is also very distinct.

In Wales, markings on the road are in both English and Welsh. One of the best examples of this is Araf, which means Slow. This marking is only found in Wales.

NOTE: Scottish Gaelic and Irish are both also Celtic languages. They can look somewhat similar to Welsh.
